mother and the fetus (see Chapter 18). Poor outcomes are also 
common in obese teens who become pregnant. Many teens 
enter pregnancy with suboptimal nutritional status, especially 
for iron, calcium, and folic acid. In one study, women in the 
United States who gave birth as teens were more likely to be 
overweight or obese as adults (Chang et al, 2013).
Improved dietary practices can be one of the most important 
factors for the pregnant teen. In counseling young mothers, the 
nutrition professional must be aware of the teen’s psychosocial 
and literacy levels, her economic status and level of independence, 
as well as her cultural environment, all of which may influence her 
food choices.
